utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Madam Registrar. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, ma'am. All the accused are here. Same for the Defence teams. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls, and Mr. Thayer. Witness number 101, PW-101 is present in the courtroom. Are there any preliminaries? I take it that there are none, so I can proceed with the witness. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I wish to welcome you to this Tribunal and to this case in particular where you are giving evidence. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of a solemn declaration, promising that you will -- undertaking that you will be testifying the truth. Please stand up, read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So before you start giving evidence and you will be asked questions first by Mr. Nicholls, I wanted to confirm with you that we have put in place for you two protective measures; namely, the use of a pseudonym and also facial distortion. I just wanted to make sure that these are to your satisfaction. Mr. Nicholls will go first, who will then be followed by the Defence teams on cross-examination. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning and thank you, Your Honours. If I could first hand the witness the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, I want you to read that quietly to yourself, not out loud, and just tell me, is your name printed on that sheet of paper which will be P02448 under seal.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could that be shown to my colleagues, please. And Your Honours, could we please go into private session for some background material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I now want you to focus your attention on the period of July 1995, and do you recall the date of the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, ever since I established contact with you, I guess because of everything I have experienced, I developed some kind of an antagonism towards that date. I had to learn that date as a parrot because I simply had to know that it was around the 11th, 12th, 13th, 14th, and 15th, those days. Now, as to what date it was involving me, I think that this was two or three days after Srebrenica was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You're moving a little bit ahead. I was just asking you now if you remember the date; and if I'm right, you don't remember the exact date, is that what you're saying, that Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: I've just told you. When Srebrenica fell, what happened, where I was a participant, took place two or three days or maybe two days after the day Srebrenica fell or was liberated, depending on how people term it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, witness, let me explain to you a legal matter that arises out of the debate that we've had in private session, and also in the wake of a particular rule of evidence that we have. I would imagine that you may be asked questions which, upon answering, there could be the possibility of you incriminating yourself. If that is the case, I don't know if that will be the case or not, if that is the case, according to a particular rule of evidence that we have, you may ask to be exempted from answering such questions. However, the right to ask for such an exemption does not entitle you to an automatic exemption. In other words, the Trial Chamber, us, the four Judges up here, we can, after hearing what you have to say, compel you to answer the question or questions that may be. However, there is a legal guarantee that is provided for in the rule in your favour in such a case, if we compel to answer such incriminatory questions; that testimony compelled in the way, in this way, in other words when we force you to answer the question, shall not be used as evidence in any subsequent proceedings against you for any offence, except if you are charged with false testimony, with perjury. Do you understand me? Do you need --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But as we go along, if this becomes too difficult for you to understand, and you need further clarifications from us, we have got all the time to explain these things, your rights in particular to you. You have not been treated as a suspect by the Prosecution, but some of the Defence teams seem to think that you should have been. So you will probably be asked questions which potentially, potentially, could lead to information that could become incriminatory. You can ask us to exempt you from answering those questions. We can decide not to exempt you. If we decide not to exempt to, then that evidence will not be used in any criminal proceedings against you, except if you are caught here perjuring yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I am sorry for this rather long interruption. Mr. Nicholls, you will agree with me it was all for a good cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I do agree, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, my next question concerns your knowledge of any prisoners in the Zvornik area after the fall of Srebrenica. Do you recall Muslim prisoners held in Zvornik shortly after the fall of Srebrenica, and if you will tell me where that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Finish your question and -- but don't answer the question before we tell you, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if so, if you could tell us where those prisoners were held?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we believe that this is a leading question, and my colleague was leading the witness from the beginning. Of course, that was for identification purposes, absolutely no problem with that. But as regards the substance of his testimony, we will be insisting with this witness, due to the nature of his am testimony, that there is no leading. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is leading because it ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you -- I think Mr. Bourgon's objection is well-founded. You need to rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm trying to frame the topics but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the same time, we'll -- we'll get to the same area in any case, Mr. Bourgon, so let's be practical about it. But go ahead and rephrase your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After the fall of Srebrenica, do you recall seeing Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Can I simplify? They were not just prisoners, rather, in the course of the day -- let me tell you, the nature of my work was such that I was constantly on the move with my van. I was an errand boy, so to speak. I had to all kinds of thing, so I was on the move constantly. When I came to the barracks to get fuel or to report, to say that I completed my previous task and needed a new one. Any time I came -- or rather on that day when I came, I saw some buses, buses from various cities, licence plates from various cities, parked in the barracks compound with prisoners on the buses blindfolded and with ligatures on their hands. I saw them being taken out in groups of ten to 15, being taken to the toilets inside, and then taken back to the part of the barracks compound where Serbian soldiers were held in custody if they had violated some rules. There was room for 130 people, and there were about 20 to 30 there. People from Srebrenica who were wounded, and also those who were not wounded. And they were kept there because they were important people who knew a lot and were brought there for interrogation. I don't want to say anything but the truth. Neither I nor anybody else in the barracks ever heard that these people were ever mistreated, no moans were ever heard. The door to this conference room was always open. They sat there talking, and I came to inquire out of curiosity for two or three drivers, who were my colleagues who used to be my colleagues in Centrotrans, and I came to inquire to see how they were. They gave me an answer and that's how it was. In that group, there was a man from Tuzla --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there for a moment, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If he stopped him from rambling, then I don't have an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I object to the characterisation as rambling. It was an answer. It was a long answer but it was detailed answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not get keyed up on the use of the word rambling. He hasn't mentioned the location of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That was what my next question was going to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you talked about the barracks where these buses were and where the prisoners were held. Can you tell me the exact location of the barracks, which barracks are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Am I supposed to say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, please, if you can tell me the location, the town, which brigade these barracks were a part of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: All this while I was talking about my brigade, my barracks, the only one in the area of Zvornik and the environs. That's at Karakaj, the so-called Standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't want this to be in private session or...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think this is all right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you tell me approximately how many buses, you might have said it and I apologise if you did, but approximately how many buses you were talking about that you saw at the Standard barracks in Karakaj? Just asking you how many buses.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: On those occasions I would come to the barracks, it may have been one, two, or three times a day. As for the rest of the time, I was attending to different errands elsewhere. Every time I came there, there was a different bus with different registration plates, but the prisoners were taken out the same way as I described before, to go to the toilet, and I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you can tell me which unit of the Zvornik Brigade was guarding the prisoners when you saw them being taken into the Standard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: They were police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Military police or civilian police, just to be very clear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Nicholls. Let's go into private session for just one question that I would like to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I have a new topic. In 1995, as a soldier in the Zvornik Brigade, did you ever see the chief of security for the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Quite a few officers from the corps or staff, whatever it is called, passed through Zvornik. They'd come in passing, pull up in their cars outside the command, do their business there, and leave. I didn't know anyone. I knew those people in the corps who I had dealings with. They were mostly people from the logistics service. I knew a couple of officers there. I am not sure if you're asking me about someone specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the corps at this moment. What I'm asking you about is if you knew -- if you saw the chief of security for the Zvornik Brigade, if you would see him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: I am not sure who you're referring to. If you told me his name, I'd know. This chief of security, was he -- well, he was stationed definitely at the corps facilities. He was definitely not in Zvornik because the junior officers were down there, including officers for security. Am I supposed to tell you his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Tell me the names of the security officers you knew who were attached to the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: I only knew Drago, or Dragan, Nikolic; I believe his name is Dragan Nikolic. I knew him because he spent a great deal of time at the barracks, and I'd come across him just as anyone else. I knew him personally as a decent person, a pedantic person. He was rated as an officer who wasn't arrogant or taxing on anyone. I knew that he was in charge of security because everyone talked about it. He was in charge of the exchanges between Serbs and Muslims. I heard that he was very successful in what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you as a soldier, when this person Drago or Dragan Nikolic from the security section came by, would you have to do anything when he passed you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: No. Out of respect from -- for his rank and his duty as an officer, I wouldn't really greet him or salute him in the military way. I had respect for him as a person as well, and I would greet him amicably. I was never in a situation to broach a conversation with him. He never addressed me as (redacted), how are you doing" either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's stop there. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, Witness, let me just tell you to put your mind as rest, as I told you before, I think, there is a 30-minute delay before anything is broadcast outside the courtroom. So be very careful about what you say, but His Honour was able to catch that and it will not be broadcast. Do you understand? I just want you to be at ease.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I want to move on. I'm not talking about the prisoners at Standard and Karakaj anymore. New topic. After you had seen the prisoners at Standard as you've described, the next day where did you go, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: The following day -- you're asking me as if it happened yesterday, the day before yesterday, or seven days ago. It was ten or 11 years ago. I told you that I was always on the move in my vehicle. I don't know in which part of Republika Srpska I was on that day, but I know that on the day the event took place I was -- I arrived at the barracks in the early evening hours. At that point, I was assigned to do the job which eventually led me here to sit before you. That was in the evening hours. I don't know where I spent the rest of the day, and I'm not sure if you are interested in hearing about it. These were different errands I had to do; for instance, transport the wounded to the military medical academy at -- in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you, sir. Now, when you went to the barracks in the evening hours, were you given an order to go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's a leading question. Please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What happened after you went to the barracks in the evening hours? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: That bit I know, and I will remember for life. As I came there, I was given the task from Chief Pantic to park the car within the barrack compound next to the entrance and gate. I was told that cargo boxes with cookies, doughnuts, and other pastry, including boxes of juices and mineral water would be brought over. There were also two sacks, paper sacks of bread. I was given the travel order to transport the goods to the school at Orahovac. I did that without knowing what was happening up there, and I got into the car and went there. Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, please. And -- yeah, please continue. What happened after you went there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: I got to the school, I saw this other section of the school further up, and there was a large group of soldiers. I thought something was going on up there, and I presumed I was supposed to get there. I parked my van, got out; and without knowing at that point what was going on, I saw soldiers, military police officers. I saw the Deputy Commander for logistics. Should I say his name? May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Sreten Milosevic. I saw him in the group of people standing out in the street. They weren't doing anything in particular. They were conversing. There were many other soldiers there and junior officers whose names I cannot tell you, although I would if I could. There was this private businessman who was very of a fluent, (redacted). He was a financial businessman. He was wearing civilian clothes and carrying a rifle. I was surprised to see him there because I never saw him participating in matters such as this one. I can still didn't know at that point why they were there. I opened the back door to the van where the food was. The soldiers were around and Sreten Milosevic said, "Help yourselves." And they each approached the van and took what they fancied. Some took juices, some took savory food, others took pastry. As far as I know, two sacks of bread were taken to the hall there. I still didn't know why at that point. So two sacks of bread were some 40 to 50 kilograms of bread.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Mr. Nicholls, you either control your witness yourself or we will do that. We usually try not intervene as much as we can, but you objected to a particular word that was used by Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was, Your Honour. I'm...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: First of all, may I request the redaction of the name at line 25 of page 18, the name of this person, this businessman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask why?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Because I think the witness's testimony of speaking to this particular person could lead to knowing who the witness is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree. Mr. Bourgon, isn't that convincing enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I don't know. This -- I know the name, but the fact that this name is mentioned, that he had a conversation with the witness, would allow maybe that person to identify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That person can spill it out to everyone then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our decision is to redact, and we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I just say that one of the sort of traditional bases for allowing some leading questions is to assist in focusing the witness. If I can't lead at all, then it may make it more difficult. I'm just trying to lead on basic topics to frame them for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I see that the notes mention several names in addition to the one that was redacted. One of the names there may be a potential witness, I believe one of them is already on the list, and so I don't see any reason why this name should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has already been redacted, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. I -- my colleague, Mr. Nicholls, mentioned leading questions. My objection wasn't necessarily to the leading questions; it is to the nature of the answers. They become rambling and it's not proper. I think Your Honours have just seen that. Of course, I also object to the nature of the leading questions one at a time, but my other objection was the nature of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The position as received is very simple. I have sensed that Mr. Nicholls has been put on notice by you not to put leading questions with this witness. If that is the case, then obviously a measure of free-lance has to be allowed to the witness; then we usually don't intervene. It's up to the counsel, up to counsel to regulate the -- his own witness. I mean, what we told Mr. Nicholls is that at any time he feels that the testimony shifts from what is relevant to what is not relevant, he is free to -- to stop him. Otherwise, if it comes to a stage where we believe it's irrelevant, then we will intervene. But as long as it is relevant, I have no objection with the witness -- we have no objection with the witness going on and give explanations rather than answer questions. I mean, there have been trials that have been conducted that had way throughout here. You know that. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go into private session please, for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you have explained about arriving at the school in Orahovac and what's happened up to this point and a conversation you had. What happened next? What was the next event that you observed at the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: I saw something, and I told about this in the statement. As I was there, as the food was being distributed, I stood there inquiring who this was intended for, what was going on; and then they told me that there were prisoners there who were going to be exchanged. They were Muslims and they were imprisoned and then they would be exchanged. And as they were helping themselves to the food, a truck arrived. I think it was a Zastava make. This truck arrived from the direction of Krizevci and Kitovnice. It came in front of the school, turned around, and stopped there; then the policemen got active. They created some kind of a corridor, the policemen and soldiers, and then some policemen went to the gym; and then they took a certain number of people. As they got closer to the truck, I could see that there were 20 to 25 of them with blindfolds and their hands tied. They yelled at them, screamed at them, "Hurry up." I don't know what else they were saying. They put up some sort of ladder for them to climb on to the truck. As they were approaching this small column, as it was approaching, some of them probably had doubts, or rather, had fear that something worse would happen and some of them started fleeing -- or rather, one of them started fleeing; and then by the time he realised in which direction he should flee, the soldiers caught up with him and they started shooting, or rather, I could hear bursts of fire behind the building and then the soldiers came back without him; and then they continued getting prisoners on to the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment, please. Now, was there anyone issuing orders to the military policemen during the transport of these prisoners on to the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Let me tell you something. I saw Sreten Milosevic who was a senior officer. He was in charge of logistics. He was not a type of officer who was qualified for police and special military formations. He really wasn't competent in those kinds of assignments, and he stayed there the whole time by the road. He was there by the vehicles, by the van. And I'm sure there were others there, other soldiers and other officers, who organised the work in the sense that the people had to be taken out. Now, who coordinated that entire work, I don't know. I didn't see. Under the circumstances, I could only focus on certain things, and I was, in a way, interested in certain figures, but not in all of the events. I'm sure that there was a junior officer there or a non-commissioned officer who organised that. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a minute. Which VRS officers were at the school in Orahovac that you saw? Think carefully. Answer carefully. Tell me the names of all VRS officers you saw at the school in Orahovac that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: I saw Sreten Milosevic, Drago Nikolic, who was not in that section by the road. I'm not sure it's Drago or Dragan. I think it's Drago. I have a lot of nicknames myself. I think his name is Drago. He was there listening and issuing orders and other people were carrying out his orders. And I think that there were some non-commissioned officers, some sergeants and, you know, people like that, but I'm not very knowledgeable when it comes to ranks and tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would like to show you, please - and this can be broadcast - number 1691, that's a photograph. It might take a couple minutes, sir, but you should see a photograph appear on the screen in front of you. If you tell me when you see it, please. I know it takes a while, but I have a hard copy if there is a problem. Although, I would possibly like the witness to mark it, so it would be better on e-court. Maybe we'll come back to that. I'll ask you some more questions, Witness. You said in your last answer the person Drago or Dragan Nikolic, you think his name is Drago Nikolic was there listening and issuing orders and other people were carrying out his orders. Explain that a little bit, who you saw him issuing orders to and what they were doing in response to his orders, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Let me tell you, those were not really orders. I think that they planned and coordinated how to do it systematically. There was no need for him to constantly give instructions. People knew it; it had been all pre-planned. As I told you, I was on the road, Drago was there; and then there was a fence; and that there was the gym; and then a hall in front of the gym; and then there was a door which was closed. And I don't know how many of them there were inside, them and the policemen and soldiers. And then just to give you a details, they took water to them in jugs, and distributed water to them. So it all seemed normal to me, under the circumstances, which were very difficult. They needed to take water to these people. But I was unable to see anyone inside and recognise anyone, including policemen, soldiers or non-commissioned officers, sergeants, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, tell me more about the process of prisoners being put on the truck. You started saying that they were taken and climbed up some kind of steps or platform. Can you explain that. How many prisoners got on the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: I don't think that more than 25 can fit. It's not that they just sat on benches, no. They also stood next to each other. In my view, 25 to 30 people. To tell you the truth, in such a difficult situation, one doesn't really care about numbers.

utterances.text: Okay. Do you intend to have the witness mark, put markings on this photo, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.text: I did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can have the break as you suggest now. It will be 30 minutes also because we need to discuss a few things. And we will reconvene soon after. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you see a -- are you okay, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you see a picture on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you tell me what is shown in this picture, what building is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: To the right is the school building. Next to the school building is the gym with an entrance and everything else that is needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be very clear, which school is this? Do you recognise which school, which town this is in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: This is in the village of Orahovac --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: -- near Zvornik; five kilometres from Zvornik, or six.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you talked about the truck that the prisoners were loaded on to.
