And the court officer will give you a stylus - it's like a pen - and if you can put a mark where you saw the truck approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Yes. The truck, on its arrival, turned around. It was facing Krizevci, and it was right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: My van and I were here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. That's enough. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I can say for the record, the X on the lower portion of the photo, the witness stated was where the truck was when the prisoners were loaded; and the other marking above it slightly to the right is where he stated his van was parked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Witness, could you please just write, let's say in the top left corner, 101, your number. Photo, 101.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm done with that. That can be taken off the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I just have one follow-up question. You said earlier that the soldiers and the police, when the prisoners were loaded on to the truck, were yelling things, "Hurry up, hurry up, get on the trucks," things like that. Were those military police or civilian police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Not civilian. Military.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'd like you to continue, tell me what happened next. What happened after you saw these -- I don't remember the exact number you said, and it -- I don't expect you to remember the exact number. But after the prisoners were loaded on the truck, what happened next? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: I saw the people being put on the trucks. The truck started; and when it was on the road, a jeep started riding behind it. Inside there were soldiers with open doors, ready to intervene should somebody decide to jump off the truck. I was told to ride behind them until we reached a certain place where I was supposed to unload the rest of the juices and food that I had my van. So we arrived up there; the truck stopped. The police and soldiers - I don't know - had more of a fierce attitude as they were ordering them to get off. This is where the main asphalt road is for Krizanovici [phoen] and Kitovnice villages. The truck stopped there and they were getting off the truck, and it's more towards the road leading toward the railroad. They -- they marched them next to a heap of corpses, and it was then that I realised that it wasn't actually an exchange, that it was something horrible. They lined them up there. A group of soldiers, men, four, five, six of them, stood there. The others stood; and when they were given on order to shoot, they shot and the others fell; and then they took out several groups - I don't know. One, two, three groups - and then they were done with them there. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: And then in my mind something terrible, something unheard of happened. Something that I have not been able to forget until this day, and will never forget. I developed diabetes after this, just because of thinking of what a man can do to another man. This is where these people were shot to death. When giving my statement, no matter how many times you watch atrocities on -- in various movies, documentaries, and so on, no matter how many horrible books you read, books that make you cry over somebody else's fate, let me tell you it's nothing compared to what one can experience oneself, as I did there. I developed diabetes after that. In that heap, in that pile of dead bodies, who did not resemble people any longer, this was just a pile of flesh in bits, and then a human being emerged. I say a human being, but it was actually a boy of some five to six years. It is unbelievable. Unbelievable. A human being came out and started moving towards the path, the path where men with automatic rifles stood doing their job. And this child was walking towards them. All of those soldiers and policemen there, these people who had no trouble shooting -- I shouldn't judge them because I don't know about their situation. Perhaps they did it because of the order they received and perhaps they did it because of their nature. There are all kinds of people, and some of them may have done it gladly. Some probably did it because they had to. And then all of a sudden they lowered their rifles and all of them, to the last one, just froze. And it was just a child there. Had it been a person of 70 or 80 years old, it would have been horrible, let alone an innocent, sweet child. And the child was covered in bits of bowel tissue of other people. Later on in the hospital in Zvornik, the doctor showed me, he said, "Sir, this stinks." And back at the time I didn't feel the stench. I didn't even feel it as I was driving the child. I only felt it afterwards, after everything had happened. This gentleman -- I apologise, I used the word gentleman. This officer, I think he was lieutenant-colonel. I'm sure he was lieutenant-colonel or colonel at the most. I cannot get up here, although I would like to illustrate this to you. I would like to give you a descriptive impression. And he was like the most arrogant person who turned to the men, the soldiers, and said, "What are you waiting for? Just finish him off." And then these very men who had no trouble killing people earlier, said to him, "Sir, you have a pistol yourself, so why don't you finish him off. Go ahead, because we can't do that." All of them who were there were simply speechless; then the officer said, "Take the child, put him on the truck, and take him down there; and then bring him here with the next batch and then he'll be finished off." I was there. I was completely powerless. I was an outsider there, a logistics person, and I was there with a job just to keep quiet. I had nothing to do with what was happening there. They were executing people, and my job was just to bring in supplies; and then they took the child, not the men who were finishing off the people, no. The others took the child by the hand. Yes. And as the child was emerging out of the pile of those who had been executed, he was saying, "Baba," this is how they call father. He was saying, "Baba, where are you?" The child was in shock. They took him to the truck. The child, knowing that he had been on that truck earlier, started convulsing. He was shaking and saying, "No, no. I'm not going to do it." Then I intervened in order to assist everybody, including the child. And I told them, "Listen, I'll turn the lights on in my van, and I will put the music on so that I can divert his attention from all of this that's happening. I'll turn the radio on," because I wanted the child to come to his senses. He was completely lost, he didn't know what was happening and who he was. I said, "I will try to take him wherever you want me to take him." So I came into the van and I put the light on, because -- and it helped the child because to him everything was just pure darkness. And I put the radio on, the local radio station, with the music that was familiar to him, and I did this to allow him to recover, to come back to his senses. I said to him, "Come here, come here, come to me." I said, "Look. I have light on, music on." All of a sudden he took me by the hand and came to me. I don't want any one of you to experience that. I used to be a strong man. I used to be a firm man. That was my reputation. But I wouldn't wish this upon anyone to experience this -- the grip, the grip of him on my hand, and I was amazed at his strength. The strength of this child. And then I -- I got into the car, I -- I left him alone for a second, just because I had to turn the car on, and I put the music on, and then we went back with the rest - you know who the rest were - so that the next batch could be finished off. From this place, which is called Orac, there is a water source there, water fountain, known as Orac. I drove to the elementary school, to the gym. And as I was driving down there, I knew that I should not leave him there. I knew that I could not leave him there. Since I had completed my task, I distributed the food and other supplies. And I was supposed to leave the child there but I couldn't do that, and I thought maybe I should drive to the barracks in Karakaj, the Standard barracks. There was a health centre for lightly wounded soldiers or somebody who had flu, you know, who were lightly ill. At first I thought I should leave him there in the health centre. As I was driving to Karakaj, I was thinking to myself, and I was thinking, "What if I leave him there at the military facility. I need to explain to everyone how I came across this child." And I didn't dare tell people about the situation. I didn't even dare tell my friends about what had happened at that site. So I decided to go to Zvornik instead, to put him in the hospital. I knew he would be registered there, and once he was registered then there was no chance for anything else. I was aware of what I was doing. I knew that I was even perhaps risking my own life; because if that man was ready to kill a huge amount of people, then he would certainly be ready to kill. "God forbid, God forbid," I said. I can't continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I saw you rising earlier on. Is it the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. In the transcript something was omitted, something that the witness said; namely, that it was evening and that it was dusk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That wasn't translated. Page 36, line 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for pointing that out. Give me one second to make my own annotations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was in the context when the witness said that to the child that it was just pure darkness, even though it was still somewhat light. It was dusk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. It's clear enough. I think the witness concurs with that. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You said a minute ago you can't go on. Do you feel all right? Can I ask you some more questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you need a break, we'll give you a break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I didn't say -- I just mentioned my own name. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The transcript did not pick up your name. You're all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The transcript did not pick up your name, so you are all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The transcript didn't, so we don't need to redact that. But I need to make sure that the sound, video recording, including sound, if someone check on that, please; or we can redact the last part of the video. It's the safe way to go about it. All right. So please redact from lines 13 on page 38 on the video, not on the transcript, until here. That will not be broadcast. Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, you described this lieutenant-colonel as saying that the child should be shot. Can you describe him as best you can to me what he looked like, the appearance of that lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: The key element in that situation are etched, both in my heart and in my brain. It will remain there for the rest of my life. The man was taller than I am. He was tall man. He had a moustache. He was a good-looking man. Manly. He was in an officer's uniform with rank insignia, with a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you can just tell me a little bit about his build. Was he thin, was he large? Just a little bit more, as that's the only thing I think you haven't really described.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Well-built. Well-built. When I said tall, I meant that he was bigger than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just for the record, when the witness said "well-built," he held his hands out at his sides to indicate that. You talked about - I'm sorry. I know this is difficult perhaps for you - about the prisoners being shot in one, two, or three groups. Do you remember, as much as you can, how were they shot? Were they shot individually? Were they shot as a group? Did the soldiers act on their own? Just describe as much as you can remember about how the executions were actually carried out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: You know what, earlier when I said that some of them -- and I don't know any of those men. But on the basis of their conduct during the execution, during that event, one gained an impression that some of them did it gladly, as I've told you earlier. And some did it because they had to. A detail that was terrible for me once it was all over - naturally, I've seen this in movies and so on - I guess later on those who still gave some signs of life had to be finished off. One of the guys who was that type of a person, and he saw somebody's toe stirring, and I don't know how to describe it to you picturesquely, his attitude, his words. He was saying he needed to go and killed that toe. You know, it wasn't the head or any other body part; it was just that this toe bothered him and he had to finish him off. And I think that in that terrible evil he could have acted more humanely, you know, not be bothered by that toe or perhaps a strand of hair that was blown by the wind. I don't know. Perhaps I would not have developed diabetes, but perhaps it would seem natural to somebody else. But this was my impression, this was my experience of this event, and I will always carry it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's perhaps being a bit overcareful, but could we redact what he just said (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I apologise to you. Yes, I think we better redact that. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said you weren't sure some of the soldiers might not have wanted to fire. They were doing it because they were under orders. Was there any order to fire given?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who gave that order to fire on the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: I apologise. A moment ago I forgot to give you this one detail, and thank you for reminding me. This is contained in my statement. At the time when this whole story about the child was discussed, whether the child should be put in the van, a young man approached me. He had curly hair, and I didn't know him. And he said to me -- I said my name again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't hear it, but -- I didn't hear it. I don't think -- yes, yes. But let's be cautious, and let's redact these two lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will block the broadcast of those two lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for bringing that to our attention. Please be careful and continue what you were saying about what this young man with curly hair said to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I apologise. He addressed me by my name and said, "Believe me when I tell this to you, I did not have the strength to shoot at them. I shot above their heads." And I will remember this story always. I will never forget. Why did he tell me this? What drove him to tell me this? I never had anything to do with this young man. Since he addressed me by my name, he probably knew me. But there was this strong urge within him probably to tell me this, to vent it out, to find comfort in telling me this. This, what I experienced, led me to conclude that some of them were ordered to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I had asked you was there an order to fire given, and you said, yes. My question is: Did you hear or see anybody give an order to fire? Try to remember.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: The only thing I can tell you, and I apologise for having to say it this way, perhaps. I wasn't there to follow what was going on and memorise the details. I was focused solely on the people who were standing there, who were supposed to live their lives out, to breathe, and they were all to perish. I don't know who ordered this, whether it was one of the officers from the Zvornik Brigade. Don't hold it against me, the fact that I was not in a position to observe that because this went on the whole day, and I don't know whether it went on for one or two days. I also forgot to say a moment ago that this young man wasn't brought in in that group of people that I observed arriving and getting off the truck and going on to the execution site. This child was not among them. He had probably arrived earlier. This is what I forgot to say earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me make sure my question was clear, and it may not have been. I wasn't asking you if you knew who had given the order that all of these people should be murdered at some point. Maybe I could ask my question more clearly. At the -- when you were at the execution site, did you see or hear anybody there just give the order to fire for the particular prisoners that were killed when you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: You see, nobody was able to issue orders, nor was there anyone who was senior in rank to those two men there. One of the two was, but I told you that I can't remember which one. Only the two of them were in charge there, and the only ones issuing orders. I believe that the person holding the higher rank was the one issuing orders, because he was the one who said, "Well, what are you waiting for? Finish him off;" meaning the child. Because had it been the brigade person, then he would have approached the lads there and told them the same thing. I base my conclusion on the fact that he said, "Finish him off," loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you said there were two men there with rank, and that it wasn't the brigade person who said, "Finish him off." Who was that other person with rank, who was the brigade person there? What is that person's name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: That was Drago Nikolic. I don't know what his rank was. I know it was relatively high. He wasn't a non-commissioned officer. He was a commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you have explained what this lieutenant-colonel was doing. Best you remember, what was Drago Nikolic doing when you saw him at the execution site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: He was there because the men who were escorting prisoners from the trucks, he was to direct them. Because the other men who were there were executing people, firing at them, and that was their job. Whereas, Drago was with these others. He wasn't yelling at them or anything of that kind. He was simply directing them what to do. Although the prisoners who were getting off the trucks did not do anything in particular, and there was no need to intervene in their regard. When they were taken out of the gym, they were told to be careful not to spread panic, that they would be going for an exchange, that they would be exchanged for the -- the soldiers of the other side. And for that reason, they were not worried. They maintained their calm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go back --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's addition: They were misled this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go back to the child that you told us about that you took to the hospital. You have described him as being covered in pieces of bodies, if I can say it that way, of persons who had been killed. What was his physical condition? Had he been hurt in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I forgot to mention this. When you compare it to a handyman, a person working on a house plastering the walls and the way the person is sprayed upon one's own clothes with dust and everything. Here you had clothes covered in bits of tissue and blood-stains; and then dust all over it. So there were these dark stains all over him. He was also hurt. I knew that it wasn't his tendons or anything of the sort that were injured because he was able to walk. I gathered the extent of his wounds only when he was treated by the doctor who had to stitch him up. He was lucky that none of the wounds went as far as into his bones. Should I continue with my story?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to now take you back to when you take the child into the hospital of Zvornik. Can you tell us what happened, just briefly the process of what happened when you brought the boy in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: I took him right to the entrance to a surgical ward. The child grabbed my hand tightly, and I told you already about the grip, his strong grip. And he kept saying, "Baba, please don't let them take me." And I still hear his words reverberating in my ears.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would like to now show the witness P02452. It must not be broadcast, this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a photograph in a minute, Witness. I would like you to take a minute and look at that photograph, Witness. Do you recognise anyone in the photo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: I don't know the two adults. If you're showing me this photograph to tell me that this is the boy, I'll tell you only one thing: Based on the colour of the hair, complexion, and face, it's a bit different. It's not the way it remains in my memory. But based on his face and build, stature, that's the child, yes. I don't know the two grown-ups there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Who is going first? So we will have a break in 30 minutes' time. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wanted to ask the Chamber the following: Since the evidence of the witness is considerably different from the information we received beforehand, could we have a break now to see what line of questioning we will take? We would indeed need the opportunity to consult with our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have anything to state about that, Mr. Nicholls, before we decide? We are not in a position to assess what Mr. Zivanovic has stated because, of course, we are not privy to the witness's previous statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, if I could be clear. One, I don't like that type of comment made in front of the witness. I don't think it's fair. Second, what I think Mr. Zivanovic, I don't believe he's implying that what he's heard today is new.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I think we will play -- we will play it based on our courtroom experience. Let's have a 30-minute break now. The break we'll have it now. 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have no objection to the break and the consultation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we better leave it like that and we will have the break now. 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who's going first? Mr. Bourgon is going first. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Are you in a position to tell me good morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: I did say. You didn't hear me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry. It wasn't picked up in the transcript, and I didn't hear it. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Well, you are addressing me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to begin, Witness, by confirming before I ask you any questions, that earlier this week you were provided with a letter which was given to you by my colleague from the Prosecution, and a letter in which I requested an interview, an opportunity to meet with you. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in this letter which you read, there was a paragraph in which I mentioned, "Having reviewed this material in addition to that provided by other witnesses who have or will appear as witnesses in this case, there are some issues we would like to clarify with you before your testimony and, accordingly, we kindly ask you for an interview with a view to discuss these issues." Do you recall reading a paragraph or words to that effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But before that, I apologise, I don't know how long before that I had your call. It was a verbal contact. It was a call from you to meet. I refused that; and then after this written contact, I also refused. If you want me to provide you with a reason ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: By all means, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Gentlemen, all of us have our own views and opinions. I'm not a lawyer, I'm a zero in a field, and I speak to you as a man. Up until the meeting with the Prosecutors on the 25th of November, I don't know whether you or somebody of your colleagues who are in the field had occasion to contact me. That was one opportunity; and then after the 25th of November, after the contact with the Prosecution, my name became familiar to you because it was included in a list. And I was expecting that somebody in Bosnia, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: (redacted), and to tell you the truth, I actually contacted them to see whether they wanted to talk to me. I know these associates, that's quite normal and natural. One of them is even a friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let's go into private session for a short while because we need to consult with you on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, the question that I just put to you was that the first witness statement you gave to the office of the Prosecution was on 25 and 26 November, and I may have made a mistake, we're talking about November 2005. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this interview, because this is not mentioned on the statement, I'd like to know where this interview took place, and maybe for this we will need to go into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I view it as completely irrelevant. Where the interview took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It may become relevant, but let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have lots of questions on the taking of those statements, and believe me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- they are relevant for credibility purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, Mr. Bourgon. We haven't acceded or we haven't agreed to Mr. Nicholls's objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now. Not yet. We are now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Witness you mentioned today that the chief of the transport section was a fellow named Pantic, and this is the same as the information you provided in your statement. I would like to confirm with you that that it was Pantic who gave you the order to go Orahovac on the 14th of July or that day, because you never mentioned the exact date. But the order to go to Orahovac was given to you by Pantic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: No. He only gave the order, and I was the one who wrote down Uzice and "loko" afterwards because the travel order is valid for the entire day. You see, there are many places around Zvornik that are called by their own names; whereas, these, the ones we are discussing here, are the -- basically the suburbs of Zvornik. I am the one who writes that down. They don't issue us with separate orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, I have moved on to another topic. I am past the work order. I am simply concentrating on the fact that that day you mentioned today in your testimony, that the order to go to Orahovac was given to you by Pantic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Sir, I speak Serbian. I told you earlier that I received my order that morning early before 5.00, before I set out to Uzice, and then based on that order I ran my errands. I received it in the morning, not in the evening when I was supposed to go where I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is something wrong, because still we had two questions and still the answer seems to be unrelated to this person Pantic. Mr. Bourgon's questions, last two questions, were very straightforward. That particular day when you were ordered, given instructions to go to Orahovac, who gave you that order? Was it Pantic or was it someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I typically receive an order in the morning as I arrive in the barracks. On this day it was on 5.00. And everything else -- once I'm done with my work, I go back to the barracks, I report to Pantic, to say here I am. And he gives me an order and I don't mean new order, no. A verbal one; and then I write it into this document. I think this is where the misunderstanding stems from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's clear enough now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to have on e-court, just to make things easier, the statement which was provided by the witness on the 25th of November, and that is a document 3D for delta, 80. The paragraphs are numbered so we can follow both in B/C/S and in English at the same time. I would like to refer the witness to paragraph 5, if we can focus on paragraph 5 of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, at paragraph 5, and I would read to you, and I would ask you to confirm that this is your testimony today, that "Rade Pantic ordered me," that is you, "to drive my van to the school in Orahovac to deliver food and juices to the soldiers there." Is that your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: I confirm every word that I said in 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. If we go on to the next sentence it says, "It was already late afternoon." Today you mentioned it was early evening. Your statement says early [sic] afternoon. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's late afternoon, at least what we have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, I got carried away. It's late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what's the difference between late afternoon and early evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's what I asked the witness. I would like to know what time it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, you asked him the question and -- Okay. Go ahead and ask him the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What time was it? Because your statement says late afternoon and today you said early evening. I would like to know what time you were given this order by Pantic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Sir, as far as I remember, I think that a time is indicated somewhere there. 2030 hours; that was that time. It was at the time when the sun went down. There was no moon up there yet, and I think that I said, I gave the time reference. 8.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So if we say dusk, would that correspond to the approximate time; the sun was coming down but it was not yet dark? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Well, I am a romantic by nature, and I know very well what a dusk is. I don't want to describe it to you. I have no ability to dim the lighting here, but dusk is the beginning of darkness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, also in paragraph 5, which is in your screen in front of you, it talks about the contents of the boxes which were loaded on your van, and it says that these boxes contained doughnuts, rolls of bread, and a couple of bags of bread, as well as in the order talks about juices. I would like to confirm that all this was indeed placed on your vehicle; the juices, the doughnuts, and the bread and the bags of bread. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Let me say again. In the car, there were, say, three crates of various savory rolls, savory pastry types, and doughnuts, crescents, cookies, and two paper sacks, the ones used by bread makers, full of bread. That's what I stated and that's what's written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You confirm that there were also some juices there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Juices, mineral water. There were three crates of that alone, and then three crates of rolls and pastry, and then two paper sacks of bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me just ask you to confirm one more thing concerning the vehicle, and I will move to the question which is my issue now. When you brought back the vehicle that night, now we confirmed a little earlier that this is at 1.00 in the morning. You confirm it is your testimony today that you met with Pantic on that occasion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Whether it was Pantic or the colleague who substituted called Miso, I can't even remember his last name. And I used to know it and provide it in all documents. Miso something. One of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in your statement, and this is -- I would now like to focus on paragraph 33 of the statement. And you testified to that effect today, that you returned the vehicle to Pantic after going to Zvornik hospital. Are you changing your testimony or do you stick to your testimony as you said earlier, that every word you said in 2005 was true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: You said that I returned the vehicle to Pantic, and then went to the hospital. It's not logical. I first went to the hospital with the child, completed everything there, then brought the car back. The car had to be washed. I parked it and then I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my question is not this. My question is: You returned the vehicle and you had a conversation with Pantic about taking some days of leave, as you discussed today. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I have some information that indicates that Pantic was not in Zvornik on -- from the 11th to the 15th of July. He was absent from the headquarters and he had been given a leave or holidays or some free time. I suggest to you that it was not possible for Pantic to give you an order to go to Orahovac that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Well, you know what, I said just a minute ago, and it's included in my statement. There was Miso there. The two of them did that job together in shifts. I don't know. One worked in the morning and the other one later. Pantic was the chief of transportation; and if Pantic wasn't there, then Miso stood in for him. Now, I can't remember whether on that day it was Pantic or Miso. Is that important?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you mentioned that every word you said in 2005 was the truth and this is indicated in your statement, and today you also said it under oath in your testimony. So I believe that it is indeed very important. You said it was Pantic. Are you changing your testimony? Are you saying that you did not tell the truth in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think he's answered this question. This topic has been gone over quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer the question. It's an important question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine. I would also like to know what the information is. Normally that's put to a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer the question. It's being put to you that although when you made -- when you gave the statement in November 2005, you were quite clear and catagoric that it was rather Pantic that you spoke to after you returned from the hospital. Now you are not so sure, and you are changing your testimony in the sense that it could have been the other one, Miso; is that correct? Or even the one that ordered you to go to Orahovac? I mean that's already been sort of dealt with. You agreed to that proposition that I have made to you, trying to reflect Mr. Bourgon's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you. In the beginning of my evidence, I said what tasks I had, and who my superior was, Pantic, chief of transportation. And everything I said pertained to him because he was the chief of transportation. Now, I didn't tell you who the other officers were in logistics, who sent people here, sent people there. I can't remember whether it was Pantic on that day. If it wasn't Pantic then it was Miso. I can't remember his last name. But the two of them were the main people in transportation. They were the ones who gave orders, not only to me, but to other drivers as well. I mentioned only Pantic because Pantic was the chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You also mentioned earlier on in your testimony some more details. You gave more details relating to your return from the hospital. Because you stated earlier on that when you returned to barracks from the hospital there you met Pantic, who didn't know about your story, and you asked him for three or four days off, which I understand he gave you. Did you actually -- do you confirm that the person you met after your return from Zvornik hospital and who granted the three days was indeed Pantic, or could it also be Miso? This is what we want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was my mistake that throughout the time -- you know how it is when you are a driver and you spend your entire life behind a wheel, and I'm not experienced in talking. I should have said either my chief or his deputy; one of them. That's what I should have said, but I didn't. And you know very well, you know full well who was on duty that day, because you can find their signatures in various books, logbooks, documents, and so on. I don't know to what extent it's important to you. I don't wish to lie. I don't wish to blame anyone. Perhaps it wasn't Pantic. At any rate there was a chief there. I came there, left the vehicle, I asked for some days of leave. If Pantic wasn't there, then the other one was, the one who substituted for him. Nobody else did that job but the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I would like you to refer to 3D79, seven nine, on the -- and my question is quite straightforward. Pantic was the chief of transport. MR. BOURGON Sorry. We have to go in 1D217. 3D79 is not -- has not been released, but it's the same document that was released by another team. 1D217.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, did you know that the chief of transport that you saw every day, as you say, that his mother had died during that time-frame, immediately in July?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Registrar, please attend to the redaction that we need to make. I suggest lines 23 to -- 23 to 25 on the previous page, and lines 1 and 2 of the present page. Okay. Go ahead, Mr. Bourgon I'm sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One rubs the other back, so it --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We are not in private session. We are in open session. Let's go into private session, and straight away. Redact also lines 8 and 9, please, from page 83, and I suggest you put your question again please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, first, before we move to the next individual, I'd like you to confirm whether or not the Prosecution - because this is a Prosecution exhibit I just showed you - whether this was mentioned to you that Pantic was away from the headquarters on the 10th to the 15th of July. Did that information -- was that provided to you by the Prosecution when you told them that Pantic gave you the order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: No. The Prosecution never told me that Pantic wasn't there. We didn't discuss whether he was there or wasn't. I simply said that the chief of transportation service and Miso stood in for him. So if it wasn't Pantic issuing orders, it was Miso.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, you spoke today in your testimony of Sreten Milosevic and, actually, you said he was the logistics man in the Zvornik Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I have some information which comes from Sreten Milosevic, and this information is -- suggests the following proposition to you: Milosevic has provided some information, and I'm quoting from information available to the Defence, that "in the army storage and in provisions, there were never any fruit juices in 1995." Who is correct, Milosevic about the juices or you say that there is no juices or you say that there are juices?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to rephrase it. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is an improper question. The person he is referring to is on witness list. There is no problem with him giving the proposition. I did not stand up right away. The Court, Your Honours have made this very clear that witnesses are not to be pitted against each other in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I just--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One minute. Mr. Bourgon will rephrase his question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer? No need, I can answer loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I drove juices and 200 to 500 kilos of meat to soldiers, to kitchens. Where they had come from, from stores, from private individuals who donated that in order not to serve in the army, I wasn't interested in that. But it was loaded in there, and I would wait until it was taken out of the barracks and loaded into the car. And sometimes I would even go to some stores because I was told go to that store, take this from them; go to this private butcher, take this from them; go to the Vitinka juice factory and take this from them. So I would that and take it back to the barracks, and that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On the basis of this answer, Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to stop here, Mr. Bourgon and we will proceed tomorrow. Yes. The witness, I think, can be escorted. Witness, we will see you again tomorrow morning. Please, before -- one moment before you leave the courtroom. Since you haven't finished your testimony, it's important that you do not contact or allow anyone to contact you in relation to the matters that you are testifying upon, until you finish your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have a good afternoon and evening, late and early, and we'll see you tomorrow morning. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just if Mr. Bourgon could provide me with a list of documents he intends to use on cross per our practice here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was provided with a list, but it's nothing but witness statements and information sheets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- sorry. But this is not -- this is incorrect. Those documents were released, and the Prosecution has been informed that these documents would be used on cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm talking about Prosecution document P 311, P 295, as well as a document concerning the roster and the attendance record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We must not take time from the Prlic trial, so please try to liaise amongst yourselves and we will come back tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 23rd day of February, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
